utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And as I undertook yesterday for the general, I have a copy of his Defence statement in his own language. If I can ask Mr. Registrar to assist me. That may help him. And just two small things out of courtesy to Dr. Karadzic. The document -- one of the documents I read from yesterday, P5583, I wasn't able to identify the B/C/S passage I had quoted from and that was -- I have now checked. It was at page 3 in e-court in B/C/S, second paragraph from the beginning of the page. And the final thing is D3676, which the witness spoke about yesterday in answering one of my questions and addressing himself to Your Honours, is, I'd noticed when I looked at the document last night - and this is just a cross-referencing - also footnote 141 in P973 which is Dr. Donia's report. And that being said, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, yesterday just before we broke we were talking a little bit about the Supreme Command and your evidence on that from the Perisic case that meetings didn't happen according to set dates. Now, you also told the Judges in the Perisic case that these meetings of the Supreme Command were always called by Dr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he was General Mladic's only superior; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he commanded the Army of Republika Srpska through General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the regulations said. However, the Main Staff independently planned some operations in terms of military engagement and combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said that in your statement, but I want to come back to something that you said in the Perisic case in that regard. In the Perisic case, you told the Judges there that while military operations were planned outside the knowledge of members of the Supreme Command and government, and they lay solely within the competence of the Main Staff, they were planned with the knowledge and approval of the president of the republic, and you said that in your testimony in the Perisic case at transcript page 12648; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, that's what the procedure was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you just have a look at paragraph 27 of your statement for me. And have a look at the very last sentence of paragraph 27. That says: "Operations were planned without the knowledge of the members of the Supreme Command and were exclusively with the jurisdiction of the Main Staff of the VRS." Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that planning as an overall process of combat activities was something that was undertaken by the Main Staff of the VRS without the participation and knowledge of the Supreme Command. As for approval --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you just let me get to the end of my -- the question and then I'll give you every opportunity to make a full answer. And I'm going to quote to you what you said in the Perisic case from 12648.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to see the passage. Shall we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. In the Perisic transcript, Your Honour; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. You quoted a sentence, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't quote it. I wanted to quote the exact sentence now just for clarity for the witness. It has a Defence ID number, which Mr. Reid will be able to find for me in a minute. 1D26013.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the sentence that you said, that you gave to the Court in the Perisic case reads, General: "The operations lay solely within the competence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's read out from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Lukic: "... can you tell me, was there," and he was referring to the Supreme Command, "was there a debate on military operations of the VRS, and were decisions taken about the VRS military operations at these meetings of the Supreme Command?" And your answer was: "In principle, no. Operations were planned outside the knowledge of the ... Supreme Command and government. The operations lay solely within the competence of the Main Staff, with the knowledge and approval of the president of the republic."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it is correct. However, the president of the republic could occasionally authorise the Main Staff to carry out operations independently for which he believed were urgent and necessary, and those needed to be implemented without consultation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the course of your service as defence minister, you attended a number of Supreme Command meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you said in principle the operations were planned outside the knowledge but with the knowledge and approval of the president of the republic in principle. Then your statement in your statement, para 27, that operations were planned without the knowledge of the members of the Supreme Command is an incorrect statement in principle. If you could clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Planning combat operations was exclusively done within the Main Staff of the VRS. As for approval to initiate an operation, it was in the hands of the president of the republic, i.e., the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic. It happened that the president of the republic, i.e., the Supreme Commander, Dr. Karadzic, was abroad. Under such circumstances, it wasn't possible for the Main Staff commander to meet with the Supreme Commander, and he had Dr. Karadzic's approval to act independently under such conditions and carry out certain operations should there be sudden attacks or breakthroughs through the VRS lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just with regard to the Supreme Command meetings that we've been discussing, could you tell us where are the tape recordings, the transcripts of those tape recordings, and the minutes of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was a member of the Supreme Command, as the minister of defence, I didn't know where such material was left. I suppose it was stored in the president of the republic's cabinet, that is to say, in the office of the Supreme Commander. However, I really don't know where it was kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another document, and it's a military document, D325. It's the combat readiness report of the Bosnian Serb Army, dated 1 April 1993. If we could in this document, please, go over to page 7 in English and page 8 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under the heading "Command and Control," I'd like to draw your attention to the fourth full paragraph on both pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, I think you might, Mr. Registrar, have to enlarge the Cyrillic version a little bit more, and it's the fourth full paragraph I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph, General, is a retrospective and it talks about the past year, and it begins with: "We have carried out individual and concerted battle operations according to a single design and plan, entrusting subordinate commands with detailed or overall missions as appropriate." And then if we step over to the next paragraph, you can read the rest of paragraph 4, it continues: "Over the past year, the Army of Republika Srpska has been under a single control and command structure. Despite the fact that we initially had a large number of different armies and paramilitary formations, this unity has been attained by following well-known principles such as unity, continuity, flexibility, efficiency, operationability, and security, with subordination and a single command having a crucial bearing on the relations in the command and control process." Now, General, this doesn't reflect chaos or disorganisation, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the position of the Main Staff, but they, too, say that there was a lack of unity and different armed groups and paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, General, you know your former Chief of Staff from your service in the Bosnian Serb Army came to testify here before this Tribunal, and at transcript pages 25438 to 25439, he told us in February last year about the army's communications. And on the 12th of May, 1992, General Milovanovic didn't travel to Banja Luka with the rest of the Main Staff. He remained behind to develop a schematic for the organisation of the army and to work on its communications system, and he said that the existing communications were still in place, and from that morning, on the 12th of May, even before the VRS was officially established at the embassy, he at the command post was receiving reports from subordinate units. And he was asked if General Talic from the 5th Corps, for example, needed to contact General Milovanovic that day, whether he could do it, and General Milovanovic confirmed that he could. And furthermore, General Milovanovic told us that he established push-button communications at the Main Staff so that from that day on, the 12th of May, he could get directly in touch with all the units that were going to be resubordinated to the VRS. That's not chaos, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was not in the Main Staff. I arrived only as late as July or August. I don't know now General Milovanovic communicated with the subordinate units. I do know well that the seat of the Main Staff was designated to be located in Crna Rijeka, near Han Pijesak, in an underground military facility. It used to be a reserve command location of the JNA. It contained all kinds of equipment and provided conditions for prolonged stays underground. I spent several months there as a member of the Main Staff. I know the facility very well. I had known it since before the war for over a decade. It was one of the most up-to-date communications systems within the JNA. Close by there was a repeater at Veliki Zep. Communications systems were underground so that they could not be destroyed by even atomic bombs. General Milovanovic had inherited from the JNA the entire communications infrastructure. I don't know, though, how he established specific communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, at paragraph 35 you said that General Milovanovic [sic] made public statements and public addresses to municipal leaders, and among other things, frequently pointed out that he should be president of the Republika Srpska, and I'd like to show you in that regard another document. It's P2567, and it's a note on the 42nd session of the Supreme Defence Council, dated 23 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript. There is a major difference, not Milovanovic but Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask Ms. Edgerton. Could you read the transcript, your question. "Among other things, frequently pointed out that he should be the president of the Republika Srpska." Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Mladic, and that's the reference in the witness's statement. Thank you, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, have a look at this document, which is dated 23 August 1995. At this meeting of the Supreme Defence Council -- your indulgence for a moment. President of Serbia -- and tell us when you've gone through the first page. The President of Serbia, President Milosevic, warned the people present that representatives of the international community did not want Dr. Karadzic as a negotiator because the leadership in Pale had, up until that point, rejected several peace initiatives and plans over the previous couple of years, and he turned to General Mladic to ask for his opinion as to who could represent the Serbs at the forthcoming peace conference. And we can go to page 2 in both languages. And Mladic, at page 2, talked about the attempts of "our enemies" to divide the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina into Karadzic's men and Mladic's men, which if not stopped could lead to further divisions. And if you look at the second paragraph in your language on page 2, you see General Mladic tell President Milosevic that he wished to emphasise he had no active political ambitions, that he wished to serve the people to whom as a soldier he belongs, and that first and foremost he belongs to his professions, to the army and the people, and he should be perceived solely in this light, which is, General, completely contrary to your assertion that Mladic wanted to become president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present on several occasions at the meetings of municipal leaderships at which General Mladic had contributions. He pointed out that after the war he should be the president of the republic. It was so well known to everyone in Republika Srpska, especially the soldiers. There were attempts to split up the army into two factions, one in favour of Karadzic, the other in favour of Mladic. I personally -- I was personally asked, "General, who do you support, President Karadzic or General Mladic?" I refused to state my position, having said that I have two eyes and that both are mine. By the same token, the two of them are the leaders of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they should not be set apart. That was the reason why at Supreme Command sessions I opposed proposals to have General Mladic removed as commander of the VRS Main Staff. Proposals for his removal were expressed on two or three occasions by the President of the Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. I always asked President Karadzic to present to us the reasons for which General Mladic should be removed and that we should analyse the consequences caused by his removal. I informed the Supreme Command of my knowledge to the effect that should there be a removal, there would be a conflict between the units of the VRS, which would be a disaster. President Karadzic accepted my position and decided not to remove Mladic, at least during my mandate as the minister of defence. That is precisely how things developed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in line 10 on page 10, instead of "conflict" it should be "clashes," because the witness said armed conflicts or clashes rather than conflicts in general, the stress being on "armed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, in your question, page 8, transcript page 8, line from 6: "In your statement at paragraph 35 you said that General Milovanovic made public statements and public addresses to municipal leaders, frequently pointed out that Mladic should be the president of the Republika Srpska." But I can't find the passage on the statement. If you could help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, and completely --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 34, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- my mistake, and that's -- Dr. Karadzic is right. It's in paragraph 34, the immediately preceding paragraph, the last four lines or five lines of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whole sentence -- the subject of whole sentence should be Mladic instead of Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I obviously didn't realise I had given the wrong name in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these discussions within the Supreme Command that you've just told us about, General, would be recorded in those tape recordings, set out in those transcripts and in those minutes that we discussed earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not keeping notes or minutes, and I assume that is the way it should be. I never saw such a transcript or minutes and never read any such minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was General Subotic who during your tour as your service as defence minister was responsible for recording those sessions, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Subotic recorded these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just with respect to the municipal leaders that you referred to in speaking about meetings where you were present with General Mladic, could you identify specifically one or two of those municipal leaders who we would be able to go and contact?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well this meeting at the municipality of Bileca. I remember the meeting at the Main Staff with the presidents of the municipalities of the Sarajevo and Zvornik regions. At that meeting I was present, too, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like their names. Who specifically was at those meetings and would have heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Just in line 2, it is not Bijelica, it is Bileca. The name of the municipality is Bileca. It is a transcript-related question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we can get back to it, could I have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear the answer from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I'd just like to remind him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have the specific names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot recall the names of the presidents of municipalities who were present. I didn't even know many of them. I'm not able to say except for Ratko Radic, who I know well, from the municipality of Hadzici. I also know others but I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you at least identify perhaps the year in which you might have heard these discussions, because I would like to go and look through General Mladic's personal notebook where those meetings you're talking about might be recorded?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was from September up until the end of 1992 in Bileca. At the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka, I think it was in the middle of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. At least it gives us something to go on. I'd like now to go over to paragraph 35 of your statement where you referred to Dr. Karadzic's attempt to remove General Mladic and where you say that - your indulgence for a moment - all the generals of the VRS Main Staff stood by Mladic. Now, in contrast to this, in your Perisic testimony at transcript page 12774, you told His Honour Judge Moloto that you knew that Mladic had Dragomir Milosevic arrested because he failed to support him, and he failed to sign the list in support of General Mladic. And then

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "So the correct position is that not all generals supported Mladic. There were those against him, for example, Dragomir Milosevic." And you answered: "Yes, that's correct."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statements I said that all generals in the Main Staff supported General Mladic. I never said that all generals of the Army of Republika Srpska supported General Mladic. It is correct that General Milosevic had been arrested. It is also correct that the Minister of Defence, Milan Ninkovic was also arrested by General Mladic, and he asked me to bring him medicine to Crna Rijeka, to the Main Staff, because over there no civilians who were in positions of authority could enter. I did that for him, and at the same time I asked General Tolimir to prevent a conflict between the police that was on its way with five buses from Doboj on orders issued by Minister Ninkovic, that he should be freed from the prison in Crna Rijeka, and Mladic had soldiers ready to meet this police and the two units almost clashed and that would have been a catastrophe. I asked General Tolimir that he and I try to ease these tensions. I persuaded Biljana Plavsic and he persuaded General Mladic that the two of them should meet at this place called Han Pogled and Romanija near Han Pijesak. That's where they talked, where they reached agreement. Milan Ninkovic was released. The general was also released, and there were no further arrests. And all of this is precisely a consequence of these misunderstandings and conflicts between General Mladic and Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, also in your testimony in the Perisic case, you told the Judges that you learned of the killings in Srebrenica in mid-August or the first part of August 1995, and I would like to know how did you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I had -- I held no office in the Government of Republika Srpska, and I did not have any position in the Army of Republika Srpska. In July 1995, I went to Knin with my family in two vehicles to see my parents in order to find a solution as to how to get my parents out of Knin and to see whether they could go on living there at all or not. I stayed there up until the beginning of August. On my way back by car, my driver was present and this other man with the other vehicle, as we were passing through Konjevic Polje, we went through a blockade and positions of one particular unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. We were stopped then. They conducted checks, and it was only then that they let us go. As we arrived in Pale, I found out from the media about Srebrenica. Later on, my knowledge was based on what I read in the press, heard in the media, in statements made by certain persons, and personal conversations with some generals like General Miletic. I did not take part in any way in affairs related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing, you've just said that you had no position in the government or the Army of Republika Srpska at that time, but at that time you were a member of the state committee for centralised procurement to the armed forces of the VRS, and the committee chair was Dr. Karadzic, and on the committee was General Mladic; Mr. Krajisnik; Mr. Cosic; Milan Ninkovic, who was your successor defence minister; Ranko Pajic, who was the minister of finance; and Tomo Kovac, who was the deputy minister of internal affairs. Right? At the time you were still a member of this committee.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the composition was of a temporary nature. This was no institution. It did not have a stamp or a seal of its own, and it is correct that I was a member of that team.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in June of 1992, 20 June, in fact, you were named team leader of an executive team tasked with organising and transporting ammunition for the needs of the Bosnian Serb Army from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and by the 27th of June, you were to place that ammunition in a number of agreed locations, depots, in the RS and inform Dr. Karadzic when the task was accomplished; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct that I was appointed by President Karadzic to be in charge of a team that was supposed to find possibilities for transporting ammunition from Yugoslavia to the depots of the Army of Republika Srpska. When I received these orders, I personally went to see three border crossings from Zvornik, Visegrad, and I established that at these border crossing points there was international police. On one side there was the police of Serbia, on the other side the police of Republika Srpska. I was outside the army and outside the government at that time, and I had no influence over the police. I thought that it was inappropriate for me to be in charge of that team. I returned to President Karadzic. I made him aware of the situation at the border crossing points, and I said that I cannot work on these matters. I left this order at the office of the president of the republic, and he said, "All right. You don't have to do that." And indeed, I never did that kind of work ever, up until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I just want to come back now to something you mentioned in terms of your sources of information regarding the killings of men and boys in Srebrenica. You said one of -- you learned about it in part from personal conversations with some generals like General Miletic. So what did General Miletic tell you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, all the information I received from military personnel roughly boiled down to the following: Most of the Muslim soldiers and civilians were killed during the breakthrough --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and then you may ask further questions. Please continue, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So most of the Muslim population and soldiers were killed during the breakthrough. As they had set out, several thousand of them, roughly each soldier brought his family along, too, and they started this breakthrough. They came across the combat positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, and there was a mutual exchange of gunfire, and the Army of Republika Srpska prevented that breakthrough. In this fighting it was mostly Muslim soldiers and civilians that were killed. The second piece of information I got was from Stefan Karganovic, who was a member of the commission, and he gave me documentation about Srebrenica, and it says that about 400 Muslims were executed, 400 Muslims from Srebrenica, and that there's no doubt about that. So that is this crime that was committed, whereas all others went missing or were killed during the breakthrough. From other officers I heard the same thing, that a number of Muslims were killed intentionally because of the crimes that they had committed, in Fakovici on the 7th of January, 1993, in the village of Kravica in Jezestica on the 12th of July, 1992, and in many villages in Podrinje where over 3.000 Serbs were killed before Srebrenica, and that was retaliation only, which could not have been prevented through the system of command and control. Furthermore, I found out from the team investigating crimes against Serbs that several hundred Muslims were found alive all over the world, and their names are carved in at the memorial cemetery in Potocari. I found out from the documentary film "Sarajevo 1 and Sarajevo 2," where a man of theirs who was police commander when all of this happened, I think his name is Miholjcic [phoen] or something like that, he says that Muslims in Srebrenica killed at least 1.000 people amongst themselves. That would be it basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about a couple of things that I'd like to go back to, and one of those things was the execution of 400 Muslims from Srebrenica. Now, is that -- what -- what did General Miletic tell you about those 400?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me about the number, but he said that there were intentional uncontrolled executions of Muslims as revenge because of the crimes that Muslims had previously committed in Serb villages. Also, that most of the Muslims lost their lives during the breakthrough. That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that General Miletic told you that, and I'll find your words exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He told us that it was Stefan Karganovic who was a member of the commission. What commission was it, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government of the Netherlands established an international commission that dealt with investigations of the crimes committed in Srebrenica. He was one of the members of this commission. Three times I had the opportunity of meeting him, it just so happened. He gave me reports of that commission, and he told me that it was proven beyond any doubt that 400 or 401 or 1 less than 400, I'm not sure, but anyway, that was the number persons intentionally executed. And investigators of The Hague Tribunal were also members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Executed where, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were taken to a number of locations. I believe one was toward Bijeljina, Pilica, or something. I don't remember the exact names of those places, but executions were organised outside of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that -- your indulgence for a moment. Now, it seems by your evidence General Miletic wasn't the only general you spoke with. You said you learned about the killings from some generals like General Miletic. Tell us specifically what other generals you spoke with.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak to any general, but that was confirmed by General Mladic and by General Tolimir, I believe, at some meetings. The -- I mean the centralised supply committee meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did General Mladic and General Tolimir confirm as regards the killings at those committee meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was informal conversation. I personally wasn't present and they didn't inform me of the events. In their conversations, they stated with certainty that a smaller number of Muslims was executed in retaliation of the crimes committed against Serbs in 1992 and 1993. Most of them, however, got killed during the breakthrough. That was the essence. I didn't ask any questions about that, but that's what I heard from them in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A smaller number being how many?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody has ever given me precise information except for Karganovic in his report, that is the report of that commission which I read.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when did these conversations with General Mladic and General Tolimir take place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was until late 1995 most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these were -- these were conversations in the -- in the periphery of the committee meetings or these were personal conversations? I'm not still not quite clear about this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were informal conversations during the breaks at that meeting. Somebody asked something and then the answer came, and I didn't ask anyone, but I heard the answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who asked?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall. There were about two dozen of us. Some committee members or possibly all. I really don't remember who asked the question. It's irrelevant to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is the committee -- when you talk about this committee, that's that state committee for the centralised procurement for the armed forces of the VRS that we talked about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a provisional committee, the purpose of which was to introduce order into the procurement of the VRS under the control of the highest authorities of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just one more question about this area, and it's about -- it's about the mention of the -- the 400 that you spoke about from Mr. Karganovic, the 400 intentionally killed. I want to know do you actually believe this information from Karganovic, or do you know today that, in fact, thousands of men and boys were executed in organised executions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to this day, to my knowledge it remains roughly like that. I have never received information to the contrary or different information. In all TV broadcasts and in all newspaper articles, there was always mention of the greatest number of Muslims getting killed in the breakthrough. And a number of Muslims was executed in retaliation for the crimes that the Muslims committed against the Serbs in 1992 and 1993. That's the gist of all information up to this day. There's also the information published by the commission for the investigation into crimes against Serbs, namely that they found a number of Muslims who were -- who are alive, and their identity was established, but in spite of that, their names were carved into the monument of the killed in Potocari. And it is certain that the number is not correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're repeating yourself a little bit, General. Just before we leave this area, I just want to ask you about these informal conversations, one last thing about these informal conversations with General Tolimir and General Mladic where you heard them confirm the information about the killings. Now, you said these were informal conversations during a break in that committee meeting, the committee for procurement, and you said that there was -- I'm not sure how many off the top of my head, but about a dozen people there. Now, I read you the names of the formal members of the committee, Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Cosic, Milan Ninkovic, Branko Pajic, Tomo Kovac, but you talked about a dozen people there. So who else was there at this meeting where you overheard this information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the members of the commission, assistant -- the assistants to the ministers of defence, commerce, procurement, the police were present, people from the government, and the commodity reserves, and even the managers of major companies, such as the manager of Serbian forests, so that there must have been over ten people present.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So throughout the fall of 1995, you were obviously in scenarios where you had conversations with these people and Dr. Karadzic -- what did Dr. Karadzic say about these killings either to you or that you overheard during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was it confirmed that I attended these committee meetings and that I spoke about the killings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. She didn't mean to say that you attended that meeting. Please answer the question, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know that Dr. Karadzic ever spoke to anybody about Srebrenica. I really wasn't present at any such occasion, and I have never heard a single word from him about Srebrenica. I wasn't in such a position to be able to discuss this topic with him or to be informed by him, because I didn't hold a high office. I have never heard President Karadzic putting forward any information about the Srebrenica operation or the casualties of either side there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you hear him express any view in August 1995 or after that about the tragedy? What was his view about the killings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge or memory about that. I really cannot answer. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just going to go, to conclude, back to one area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are leaving this subject. Mr. Kovacevic, you told us that the -- it was your initial information that you heard at the time that about 400 Muslims were executed, and Ms. Edgerton asked you later on that whether you stood by, in particular in relation to the numbers executed, whether you stood by that information, and this is your answer: "Up to this day, to my knowledge it remains roughly like that. I have never received information to the contrary or different information." Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I never dealt with this matter, but I did get information from various sources, including the media. Of course I cannot say the figures are correct, because it's not for me to speak about that and qualify it as true or false. I can only say what I read and heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that regard, I was wondering, Mr. Kovacevic, whether you followed some of the witnesses here at the Tribunal, or judgement delivered at this Tribunal in relation to -- or with respect to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I followed some, but I do not have a complete knowledge of everything. Certainly it is up to this Tribunal to establish the exact figures and correct information as part of the proceedings, and that should be authoritative for me and for others too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 1, the witness said, "It was not my competence." So it should be translated that. Not: "It was -- it's not for me to speak about it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It means the same thing, but, thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I might leave that area but I'd like to come back to one thing and it has to do with this committee for centralised procurement. General, that -- the task of the committee was to provide for procurement of weapons, ammunition, food, fuel, a whole range of things for the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this committee must have been involved in -- this committee, General, surely would have been notified of the massive logistic effort that it took to procure the buses, and the trucks and the fuel to move 40.000 civilians out of Srebrenica on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly no discussion at committee meetings about these matters. I now hear for the first time from you that the committee was duty-bound to find this out. It was not known to me. This is the first time I hear of it, that the committee took part in providing buses. It certainly isn't anything I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, we can have a look at a document in this regard, P4525. It wasn't a committee who took part in providing buses. The buses --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You'll have to enlarge the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The buses were ordered on the 12th of July, 1995, by Main Staff General Skrbic through the Ministry of Defence with the utmost urgency to mobilise all buses available in municipalities of Pale, Sokolac, Rogatica, Visegrad, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, and Zvornik, and your expertise in logistics -- your expertise was in logistics. Your specific brief was the procurement of goods for the armed forces of the Bosnian Serb Army, and your evidence is you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that upon the request of the Main Staff the Ministry of Defence mobilised buses, but I have no knowledge of that and was not involved. It really isn't anything I know. This is all that I can say. It is possible that these buses were mobilised. I believe that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll leave this, then, and I'd just like to come back to one area that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your last question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, but I'm afraid it would take longer than six minutes. Would you prefer that we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it is convenient. We take a break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Kovacevic. Yesterday at page 90, I believe we were close to a misunderstanding. Did you meet anybody from the Defence team but not on this occasion, I mean earlier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attorney present here. I can't recall his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you then review the statement that he compiled based on your testimony? Did you then review the transcript of your evidence and earlier statements?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We reviewed all my earlier statements that I had given to the bodies of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The statement admitted here, did it have anything to do with that interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is a compilation of all my statements given so far, but it does not include everything that can be found in my earlier statements. However, the essence is summarised in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me start with the most recent things. On page 23, a bit further, you were asked about my attitude toward Srebrenica. Can you remember what the situation was like in the other theatres of war at the time? Was there anything that was drawing my attention?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was known or there were indications that Operation Storm would begin. Such information was arriving from the Croatian side and the Muslim side, and all the leadership of the RS was focused on responding to that offensive and fending it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Strategically speaking, what was the situation of the attack on Dinara and the municipalities of Glamoc, Grahovo, and the others over there? What was its significance for the RS and for the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I really even at its broadest don't see how the strategic significance of the attacks on these areas arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it explains why they may not have been discussing Srebrenica and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be leading then. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But general said that there were indications of Storm and preparations, which has to do with the very area, with Mount Dinara and attacks on us. Storm could not take place before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. Put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did the preparatory attacks occur in July before Storm and at the time of events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Glamoc, Grahovo, Petrovac, Bihac, in that area bordering on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the importance or what would happen and what did happen once they managed to seize control of that area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Republika Srpska Krajina, it meant that they could not have strategic facilities needed for defence under their control. For Republika Srpska, it meant that whoever was in charge of those features or facilities was in a favourable position to advance deep into RS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before going westwards, and you told us today that you wanted to pull out your parents, did you know what was the envisaged scope of active combat around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was premature. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Do you remember the question, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot provide a specific answer of importance concerning Srebrenica given the fact that Srebrenica was a protected area and that the Serbs took control of that area so as to be able to move parts of forces engaged in that area to Banja Luka, Drvar, and Petrovac. That is to say, the area in which Storm was supposed to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it requires speculation, please don't, but let me ask you the following: Was the main preoccupation of the Main Staff Srebrenica or the events to the west?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you designated General Milovanovic, Chief of the Main Staff, to be in charge of defence in Bihac, Glamoc, and Petrovac, thus providing great importance and putting -- placing a lot of stress on defending that area. The Main Staff headed by General Mladic was in Banja Luka, in the centre of military schools barracks. He was in charge of these defensive preparations to defend Banja Luka. It is visible from that that both you and the Main Staff at the time focused all of your attention and all of the measures that were necessary to the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning on page 8 you were asked if the Main Staff had communication links, and it was suggested that it couldn't be described as chaos if the Chief of Staff could contact the units. Can you tell us what the capacity was and the possibility of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff to get involved in mutual relations between municipal units and authorities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly had good telephone communication with Banja Luka and the Lukavica barracks, as well as some other centres, larger towns in Republika Srpska. Cables were laid in such a way as to enable it. The centre was in Crna Rijeka near Han Pijesak where the Main Staff was deployed. I responsibly claim that General Milovanovic in 1992 had almost no communication with the units in the field, units such as battalions, brigades. For example, I can mention Cajnice where the brigade commander was Kornjaca - I forgot his first name - and he had great difficulty in establishing any kind of communication with the Main Staff. I say that because in September and October 1992, I was in the team created by General Mladic touring all units in the field. That is the source of my knowledge of the disorder, chaos, wilfulness, and how the people in those units could not navigate their situations. As the team, we provided orders and instructions to the commanders of those units on how to act and how to organise and establish their units, as well as how to exercise command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what kind of names did the units have when they were established, and when were they made part of the VRS? Also, tell us who had decisive influence before the VRS was formed in the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobilised units of the JNA later on became TO units of Republika Srpska. The units were commanded and controlled exclusively by local authorities. The brigades or battalions were usually named after the place where they were set up. For example, the Cajnik [phoen] Brigade in Cajnice, the Prijedor Brigade in Prijedor, the Mrkonjic Brigade in Mrkonjic, and so on and so forth. The local authorities and commanders of those units for the most part were the people in charge of such units, organising defence in their respective areas. Only after some six months or more did the Main Staff establish through corps commands a full line of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, after a decision was made on the establishment of the armed forces, is there a fundamental document without which the armed forces could not have been established?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed the minister of defence, I inherited the Law on the Armed Forces and the Law on Defence which I believe was put into force in late 1992. These were the two basic laws, and at the same time, the organisational establishment structure of the armed forces was created from the Main Staff down to the lowest ranking unit. The organisational establishment structure was created by the Main Staff, and it was approved by the Supreme Commander, the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic. Under the organisational establishment structure, the armed forces were planned to be established within one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was the year necessary? What was to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see how this is linked to an area of the cross-examination yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, there was a whole line of questions on command and control and the position of the Supreme Commander within the system of command and control in the armed forces. These questions are a foundation for some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if Ms. Edgerton dealt with command and control as such, although she touched upon that while reading out some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the issue of General Mladic's independence from Dr. Karadzic goes directly to the command and control, and I think these documents -- this document that he's leading up to will show the difference between the strategic and operational control that Dr. Karadzic had which we think arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That could be an explanation. Yes, I understand that. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have in e-court P03035.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the document? Can we see the stamp? Yes, the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document. It is based on this document that the establishment structure of the VRS was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, item 4. In the English it may well be on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know -- can you tell us what is the importance of this part of my decision in item 4? Which kind of authority did I retain, and what was delegated to the Main Staff in terms of strategic and tactical control?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It states that the Main Staff is in command of subordinate units, and the Main Staff is directly subordinated to the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is how it worked. You did not issue orders to lower ranking units such as the corps or brigades. Instead, it was done by the Main Staff. You had an obligation or task under the regulations to approve or authorise the Main Staff to implement certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who had strategic command and who had operational and tactical command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategic command was in the hands of the president of Republika Srpska. Operational command was at the level of the Main Staff. Tactical command was at the level of the corps and brigades.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my question on line 19, it should be "tactical" instead of "strategic." Thank you. Can we see item 6. In the Serbian as well, which is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the Main Staff created a more detailed organisational structure. Can you tell the Chamber what did I decide in item 6.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You authorised the Main Staff to determine closer organisation and establishment of units within the corps. Your decision was that the corps should be established. The Main Staff was in charge of determining closer or more detailed organisation of the corps. With respect to whether they would have three or four brigades each and what other units it would contain, as well as the levels of manning strength. That's what was decided by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if and how the issue of volunteers was regulated and their status vis-a-vis the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: While this has been going on for some time, I note in the witness's written evidence he specifically says at paragraph 17 that: "From 3 May 1992 until early September of the same year, I did not hold any military or other office, and I was not a member of any army in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So I would think if Dr. Karadzic is going to go further into this on redirect, he would be obligated to establish some kind of foundation for the information he's now eliciting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your question was whether this question was related to the time-frame after this witness had quit his position, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He's discussing documents even -- from even before the period where he has given evidence he joined any military forces. He specifically said he was not in any military or other office at this very period that this document is dated. So I don't know where this information is coming from at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us ask the witness whether he has some basic knowledge when he took up the office of the minister of defence, in particular with respect to some organisation matters. Yes, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I kindly ask you that you ask the general which position he held in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may ask that question as well, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, which position can you hold in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of the 744th Logistics Base, whose command and headquarters was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the arming of Serbs, the arming of volunteer units. The question of volunteers, was that regulated by some document before our conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had some problems yesterday as well in relation to this question, I asked yesterday, and I kindly ask the Court once again today, to have this document displayed, 08342, as designated in my statement. On the basis of that document, I can give an answer to the Prosecution and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have 65 ter 15120. Can we first see that in e-court. 65 ter 15120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 13th of September, 1991. General, can you tell us who was sending this document and what does it pertain to, and what does the preamble say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction refers to articles of the Law on National Defence. It was sent from Belgrade, and it has to do with the procedure of admitting volunteers and their mobilisation in terms of manning JNA units that were manned from the reserve force. So there were peacetime formations of JNA units that had lower personnel levels, and then there were wartime formations envisaging a considerably larger number of soldiers and officers. When mobilisation was ordered, volunteers were mobilised as well. This instruction orders that volunteers also be admitted. I, together with other officers from the command, took part in terms of supplying weapons and military equipment to these volunteers. Then they were sent on to wartime units of the JNA -- or, rather, the 2nd Military District. And they were placed under the command of these units, or, rather, the command of the JNA. I wish to note that we had six corps then, more than ten independent brigades and regiments, six logistics bases, and according to wartime establishment, the personnel levels of these units at the end of 1991 or beginning of 1992 envisaged over half a million soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. These volunteers and mobilised soldiers were deployed according to their wartime assignments and according to the establishment of these units. Within the establishment of a particular battalion, it was exactly specified how many persons would be taken in, in terms of specific military speciality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the second paragraph of paragraph 2, it says that they can come from any part of the SFRY if they are not younger than 60 or -- younger than 18 or older than 60. In view of the ethnic composition, who volunteered from an ethnic point of view into these units?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the largest number were Serbs, about 90 per cent if we're looking at the total numbers for the 2nd Military District. I know that there were volunteers of other ethnic backgrounds too, among them Croats and Muslims for the most part. These persons, upon their arrival as volunteers, were asked whether they wanted to join the Army of Republika Srpska voluntarily or whether somebody was forcing them to do that. All of those who stated that they had come voluntarily were admitted, equipped, armed, deployed in various units, and placed under the command of the JNA, and these soldiers of different ethnic backgrounds were for the most part very good, excellent, with regard to all matters, all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Can we please have paragraph 10 now. It's the last page in Serbian. The one but last. Page 3 in Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what paragraph 10 means and what it regulates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All soldiers, volunteers, regardless of their ethnic backgrounds, once they are recorded as members of the unit where they had been deployed, enjoyed equal rights -- or, rather, rights equal to those enjoyed by any other soldier or officer irrespective of ethnic background and there were no division along those lines. They also had the right to receive a salary and to have medical care and their families received assistance. Everything that these units had made available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know why this was resorted to, these regulations, these instructions in September 1991, to admit volunteers into the army? What led the secretariat, the federal ministry, to prescribe this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just an observation that the question -- any question related to volunteers was specifically limited to the issue of arming as it was referred to in the document. I used General Mladic's diary. I think in this line we've actually gone quite far in a way outside the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with the observation. Volunteers were only mentioned during the course of arming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were asked and you spoke about the security situation in your military district at the beginning of April. In terms of securing resources, relocation, et cetera, were there any orders or instructions that said what you were supposed to do with JNA resources in the areas where they might be endangered?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of March, 1992, when a member of a Serb wedding party was killed, Gardovic, in Sarajevo, blockades started on roads. Also, at the same time blockades started of all barracks and military installations in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Such a blockade had been carried out earlier on in the territory of Croatia -- or, rather, in the territory of the Knin Corps, and there was this great danger that these forces, armed paramilitary forces, would seize the military equipment and weapons that was at military facilities. Under my control, there were over 100 different military facilities, depots, containing material reserves, including food, weapons, medical material. So we had to start mobilisation, and we had to admit volunteers on the basis of these instructions, because the regular units of the JNA had been abandoned by members of the Croat and Muslim people. So some units remained with only 10 or 15 per cent of their prescribed personnel levels, say a warehouse of 2.000 tonnes of ammunition had only 10 or 15 soldiers there, and this depot would be surrounded by 100 to 200 persons, armed. That is why we were compelled to mobilise volunteers. And then we received orders to the effect that all the materiel from the JNA should be relocated from these threatened areas to other areas where they would be safe. The reason for the relocation of materiel reserves of the JNA was exclusively the fact that they came under threat. It was paramilitaries and other armed groups that threatened them at local level. The organisation of this relocation of the reserves from the depots of the logistics bases was something that I personally did. I personally led this effort. New relocations were decided upon only on the basis of safety and security regarding these resources. It had nothing to do with ethnic background. In the area of Visegrad, for example, there were locations where Muslim villages were in the immediate vicinity, but they did not threaten these reserves in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this 15120 be admitted, Excellencies, instructions on admitting volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3678, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P2833. That's a Prosecution exhibit. Could that please be displayed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this order that was sent from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the Federal Ministry of Defence, that is, to the command of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this, but this is just an accompanying document. The content of the actual mission is attached to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we haven't got much time, could you please tell us what is specified in paragraph 1. Perhaps you can tell us about this in your own words. And then paragraph 2 as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I have already replied to. Due to the threat posed to the units and the materiel of the JNA as well as the commands, an order is issued to execute the task as soon as possible, establish staffs and detachments and volunteer units, and man them with officers and other personnel from the JNA as well as their weapons and equipment. This is an order to act upon these lines and we -- so we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the variants in clause 2? What shall be done with assets that are safe or not safe, that can or cannot be defended?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the most difficult task implemented by teams headed by me. The roads were blockaded and so were the facilities, blockaded by armed groups. So ways and means had to be found for the majority of the materiel to be relocated to safe places. Whatever could not be relocated should be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page. Meanwhile, can you explain the term "safe area"? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Safe areas, the concept, the term, did not come up in the cross-examination. And just another observation, D3676, which was an associated exhibit with this witness which I spoke to Your Honours about this morning, is one and the same as this document that we see now, P2833. So we're revisiting an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, if I may reply. This doesn't mention safe areas but Serbian areas, as if the army had been relocating its assets to Serbian areas, but this says safe areas. And Serbian areas aren't mentioned at all. A safe area could also be a Muslim village, such as Sokolje, which was armed by the JNA. It was mentioned here by an officer that he gave a hundred rifles to the villages there because they were willing to defend Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, but does that term appear in the document? I couldn't locate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In clause 2 we read "safe areas" and "areas under threat." So these are the terms used rather than "Serbian" and "non-Serbian."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did General Kukanjac take any measures based by this document from the Federal Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He formed teams consisting of officers from headquarters, and mostly I was also a member of those teams who -- which went out in the field in the area of responsibility of the corps or brigade in question to establish to what extent it was safe. We spoke to the responsible persons from the villages and in populated places irrespective of their ethnicity. When we got commitments from the locals or from the municipal authorities that the JNA could relocate its reserves to their territory safely, we started relocating and transporting these reserves for the needs of the corps and units of the military district. Simultaneously, we also employed a unit from the reserve force consisting of volunteers from those localities who secured these assets from theft.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 1D9030.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, let us try to get this over as soon -- as fast as possible so that we may save time. 1D9030. Please take a look at this document. Tell us if this is familiar. But this isn't it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was looking for a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9030. That's not this document. Now then the number is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you spoke about General Kukanjac's action. It seems there is no translation. Please tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There is a translation. If we could just have a moment before Dr. Karadzic goes further with his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do read it, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated 4 April, General. That is one day later than the document that we have just seen. How does this fit in your information? What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a consequence of the order issued by the SSNO that we saw a minute ago, and this is an order to raise combat readiness in the units of the 2nd Military District. All units must be ready to defend themselves, and some units should be pulled out of garrisons and barracks. In these activities, retired military persons and citizens should also be employed. There is also a prohibition to issue weapons and military equipment to TO units, because it was a widespread occurrence -- it was widespread practice that the TO and others wanted to forcefully remove weapons and equipment of the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please briefly summarise item 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down, please. [In English] Could the Serbian page be lifted a little bit to see number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly what General Kukanjac is ordering in item 6.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's ordering that all activities of the units of JNA must be aimed at the protection of citizens of any ethnicity from the terror and attacks of paramilitaries and the negative consequences of the unauthorised decision of the Presidency of SRBiH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If this had been about to continue longer, I was going to rise on the basis that it was outside of the cross-examination, but I think Dr. Karadzic should be cautioned in my respectful submission. Just because this is redirect doesn't mean he is obviated of the need to establish foundation before putting something to the witness. Now, this witness has specifically said in his testimony yesterday that he was detained from the 1st of March until the 3rd of May, and he had -- 1992, and he had no insight or influence on things happening in the field. So knowing that, I find it odd that the witness is able to offer any comment with respect to this document which is dated during the period of his detention. So I think Dr. Karadzic should take care when he's putting these things to the witness in his redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us where you were on the 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the headquarters of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, in the Bistrik building on the square of the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you go about your duties?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to do so partly, because the headquarters was blockaded and we couldn't enter or leave freely, but a number of times with General Kukanjac I left the building in an APC to go to other facilities in the Sarajevo Sector and the sector of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just urge Dr. Karadzic to take further caution because the witness testified in chief that he was physically -- or pardon me, in cross-examination that he was physically unable to leave the building or communicate by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that's not a valid objection to a question, especially after the answer has been given that it contradicts some other evidence. If Ms. Edgerton thinks that that's important to her, she could ask when it's her turn to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
