utterances.text: That's fair enough as well. Do you object to the admission of this document, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, on the basis of its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3679, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us who Major-General Muharem Fetahagic was and what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a meeting took place between General Kukanjac and a group of generals from the headquarters of the 2nd Military District with President Izetbegovic about the situation and the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Izetbegovic demanded that Muslim generals be appointed to positions in the 2nd Military District. General Kukanjac accepted, and Muharem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The question was whether you knew that general and what ethnicity he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Muharem Fetahagic was appointed assistant commander of the 2nd Military District for political affairs. I had known him from before, and for a short while we were at headquarters, both of us. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Karadzic, as requested by Ms. Edgerton, could you be kind as to indicate to what cross-examination part your question is related to before putting your question so that we can follow more easily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it was put to you that the situation right before the war was not as you described it, that the situation was different and that there was conscious activity aimed at strengthening the Serbian people. Did you have information from the MPV about what was going on in the 2nd Military District with regard to the safety of the population and the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but where in the transcript of yesterday's proceedings, apart from the specific question about this witness's involvement in arming, does this generalised proposition appear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think what Dr. Karadzic is trying to do is address the issue of General Mladic's diary and the comment of this witness as recorded by General Mladic that he had participated in the arming of 16.000 Serbs and the question of what he meant by that, whether that was some kind of work with the SDS or whether it was part of the activities of the JNA during this period to conscript and arm Serbs for that purpose. So I think on that basis he's getting to the area that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did the MPV keep you informed of the situation and security of civilians and soldiers in the area of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received daily reports from the subordinate units, from the level of the corps about the security situation with respect to civilians and soldiers in the area of responsibility of the corps. We sent reports, daily reports to the SSNO in Belgrade, and in turn received daily reports from Belgrade, as well as orders on how to act in trying to overcome the problems in place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness be shown 65 ter 04999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a better copy, but I hope, General, you will be able to read. It is dated the 11th of April. Do you recall having received this information pertaining to the area of your corps? It is all-encompassing information, and it addresses both Serbs and Muslims without any difference.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was drafted in the command -- it was received by the command of the 2nd Military District. Such information was sent down to the corps and independent battalions and regiments, that is to say, the subordinate units. It addresses the conduct of political elements and the damage caused to the security situation and political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina by all sides and parties. I cannot read the document because it is unclear, but that would be the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that it was received by the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this document -- or, rather, information was drafted based on information received from the SSNO administration. The 2nd Military District command is what we can see on the top with the confidential number and the date of the 11th of April. So it was pursuant to SSNO information and the information obtained by the political organ and the security organ at the 2nd District Command, and it was on that basis that the document in question was drafted and forwarded to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page. Right at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the report say? Does it mince words with regards to Babic, or does it say that his further action will cause further instability? In other words, I'm trying to see whether it is biased or not, the text itself.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information contained in the text is not biased. The formation of any paramilitary formation is forbidden, including those called the Chetnik brigade of Petar Mrkonjic, which was set up by Milan Martic, or at least he tried to do so in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I be more precise, is it Babic or Martic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic. I misread the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that it was signed on behalf of Muharem Fetahagic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time General Fetahagic was assistant commander for political affairs and someone signed in his stead, although I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3676, Your Honours, which will replace the previous document which was identical to Exhibit P2833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know when General Mladic was appointed to a position in the 2nd Military District and what that position was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initial information on his appointment is something I received, and I believe I addressed it yesterday, when General Kukanjac arrived by helicopter to the barracks in Lukavica and Sarajevo. He was accompanied by General Mladic. They held a meeting at which, in addition to General Kukanjac and General Mladic, there was Colonel Gagovic and myself. General Kukanjac told us then that he was to retire and that General Mladic would be taking over his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 16806. 65 ter 16806.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in the first paragraph we find that he was appointed Chief of Staff on the 25th of April. So he was to replace General Kukanjac. On the 9th of May, he took over his duties, and on the 10th of May, Kukanjac retired, leaving Mladic in charge. Can you tell us when the decision was made on the establishment of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS was formed on the 12th of May, 1992, at a session of the People's Assembly of the RS in Banja Luka. He was appointed commander of the VRS at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did we bring General Mladic, or did we simply inherit him, so to say, at his position of the 2nd Military District commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic was first appointed by the SSNO, and he commanded the 2nd Military District until the 12th of May, 1992, when he was appointed commander of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were quite a few questions put to you about the misunderstandings between the civilian and military leadership, i.e., myself and Mladic. Did you know what President Milosevic's position with regard to our misunderstandings, whose side was he on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no occasion to obtain precise information in that respect. From my contacts with General Mladic, as well as at official meetings, I could see that Mladic kept saying that Milosevic supported Mladic and the Main Staff and the VRS as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 32379 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And apologies again. Just an observation. The area of cross-examination relating to General Mladic was about his political ambitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also you referred to General Milosevic -- or, no, President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did at a later time refer to General Milosevic in the cross-examination as one of the generals who did not support Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What better evidence of General Mladic's political ambitions than his contacts with Slobodan Milosevic in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with you, Mr. Robinson. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the next page in Serbian, please. This page in the English is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the part where Milosevic says -- well, perhaps you can tell us what was President Milosevic's position concerning the fall of Western Slavonia, I think? Who did he accused and for what? It says, "Unfortunately Ratko --" Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know nothing about this document and I would rather not analyse it. However, we can see that Milosevic is accusing Radovan Karadzic of all problems that were created. I don't think I need go any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the following page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the part where President Milosevic speaks. He says: "I think what they said was meaningless. Karadzic promised eight brigades," and so on. Could we have set aside eight brigades to defend Western Slavonia, and were we the guarantor of the Vance Plan or was it Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the guarantor was Yugoslavia and that it was expected of Milosevic to engage VJ units to protect the Serb population that was in danger. In accordance with the international community plan, it was not envisaged that the protection be provided by the VRS. That protection did not materialise from Yugoslavia. Only at the very last moment did the 5th Banja Luka Corps help a bit with receiving the Serb refugees from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we have reserve eight brigades? How many reserve brigades did we have?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic hasn't told any of us a thing about what this document is, and I think he should do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I think it is an intercept. There is a 65 ter number. A conversation between Mladic and Milosevic. Milosevic is blaming me and told Mladic all sorts of things against the leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow you, Ms. Edgerton. As a matter of principle, Mr. Karadzic should introduce what the document is about, but we all know, don't we.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I did not know what it was and the provenance, which is why I rose, Your Honour, in all honesty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the third page in the English version, and I think it is also the next page in the Serbian. The next page in Serbian, please. One more. One more page in Serbian. Page 5 in Serbian. It should be page 3 in English and 5 in Serbian. Page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We see Milosevic say the following: "Unfortunately ... you have a completely mad political leadership which is dragging you to death." That's the problem. What can you say about this position? Did he treat the civilian and the military leadership the same?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have a same -- the same position. Milosevic was more on the side of the army. We can see in this document and it is proof that President Milosevic was against the political leadership of Republika Srpska and that it provided an incentive to the arguments between President Karadzic and the Main Staff and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification following our practice.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now -- actually, did you have any knowledge as to what happened at the Sana Assembly in -- on the 15th of April, 1995? Were you informed about direct conflicts and also when I said that Mladic was acting as if he were head of state?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that Assembly, but I did hear from people who were present there that this was quite a clash between you, as the president of the republic, and General Mladic, as commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. In an evident manner, the wishes and aspirations of General Mladic became clear in terms of this struggle for power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General -- actually, I'm not going to have this called up, the record of the Assembly meeting. It's been admitted. Did you report often, on a daily basis, about the problems and obstacles you had when carrying out these relocations of equipment and weapons of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From when I was appointed to this position in the 2nd Military District on the 3rd of May, 1992, and all the way up until the end of April -- or, rather, say until the 1st of May, I sent daily reports to the SSNO, and in these reports I described the problems involved, the situation and requirements that had to do with logistics for units and institutions of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 20 it says "from the 3rd of May, 1992." Is that a mistake? When were you appointed, actually, as base commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that I was commander of the logistics base, and I sent such reports, but weekly reports with a similar content to the command of the 1st Military District, and this logistic base was within that district.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I would like to have a few significant documents admitted, those that were signed by General Kovacevic, and he describes the problems and obstacles and sabotages he encountered in carrying out his job, and I will do this through a bar table motion if it would be useful for you. We have to further questions for General Kovacevic, and we thank them for having made the effort to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I recognise the time, Your Honour, but first I think that if Dr. Karadzic wishes to have documents admitted through General Kovacevic, he has the opportune moment to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And indeed he should be doing that. And again noting the time, I would be coming back to Your Honour at whatever time Dr. Karadzic is finished with just one small request for about a five-minute re-cross on a specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can do this right now unless Mr. Karadzic has further re-examination. It's up to you whether to put those documents to the witness or not. If the requirement is met, those documents may be admitted through a bar table motion, but I cannot say a word about it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether I will have any questions depends on what Madam Edgerton would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic chooses, despite the fact that General Kovacevic is here, not to deal with those documents now, with Your Honours' permission I'd just like to re -- ask for re-cross on the small point of inheriting General Mladic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General Kovacevic, in respect of a document, Dr. Karadzic asked you whether they, I presume referring to himself and the SDS, brought General Mladic or simply inherited him, so to speak, to stay at his position of the -- as 2nd Military District commander, and that was at page 51 of the temporary transcript of today. And you answered saying, Mladic was first appointed by the SSNO and he commanded the 2nd Military District until the 12th of May when he was appointed VRS commander. Now, General, at the 50th Assembly session in April 1995 which you said you didn't attend, Dr. Karadzic spoke about his relationship with General Mladic, and I'll quote -- I'll provide the exhibit number in a moment, but I'll quote to you what Dr. Karadzic said about General Mladic coming to the 2nd Military District. He said: "Gentlemen, we got the officers we asked for. I asked for Mladic, General Ninkovic, then a Colonel, and General Perisic had visited me before that, and I had noticed Mladic's blunt statements in the newspapers." And Dr. Karadzic continued, he said: "He was already in Knin then. I took an interest in him, together with Mr. Krajisnik. I went to General Kukanjac's office and listened to him issuing orders and commanding around Kupres and Knin. We spent countless nights in the office of General Kukanjac at that time. President Krajisnik was already president of the Assembly, and I was just president of the party. I did not have any state function. We asked for Mladic and said that they should set up the headquarters as they saw fit. We wouldn't interfere." So you didn't hear Dr. Karadzic say this, did you, in front of the Assembly of Serbian people at Sana in April 1995? That's a yes or no question, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I until now I haven't heard what you've stated just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic in his question, Dr. Karadzic was actually being misleading, building a lie into his question, wasn't he, because he was suggesting to you that Mladic was inherited, right, or else he lied to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. She's asking what Dr. Karadzic's intent was in asking the question. I don't see how he can just speak to that. She can ask him what he understood the situation was one way or the other, but to speculate on why Dr. Karadzic asked a question is not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you will reformulate your question, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on what you now know having heard this quotation, do you think that Dr. Karadzic and the leadership of the SDS inherited General Mladic as he put to you, or do you think he was telling the truth to the Assembly of Serbian people in April 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated until now in relation to this question is correct. Since this is the first time I hear of this statement of Dr. Karadzic's, I assume that there were consultations between the ruling party and -- actually, the Main Board of the SDS and President Karadzic as to which general would be appointed to that position, but I really do not have any other knowledge about that except for what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the -- that comes -- the quotation I read comes from Exhibit P970, English page 324. And nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. What -- could you tell us what it is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Directly in relation to what Madam Edgerton asked just now. I wanted to ask whether that changed the fact that Mladic was appointed on the 25th of April as deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we will not allow that question. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, Mr. Kovacevic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go, but we'll rise all together. Please have a safe journey back home. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it we have a new member from the OTP today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is completely correct, Mr. President. Another lawyer who I believe needs no introduction to the Court and that is Melissa Pack. And as the Court is aware, we will not be seeing Mr. Gaynor any longer. We will be seeing Ms. Pack more regularly from this point forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milinic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milinic.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the Defence team a statement. I know a lot, and I want the truth to be learned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please speak slowly as you did just now, and also you and I should both pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D09600 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that. I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic's microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this statement and have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read the statement. I compiled it personally and I signed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page so that the witness could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature, my very own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It does faithfully reflect everything I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same as they were in this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers would be absolutely the same except that I would like to add that I'm still a professional diplomat of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Right now I'm minister-counsellor at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. I served not only as ambassador but also as consul general in Stuttgart and ambassador to Berlin, ambassador to Moscow. Right now I'm posted at the ministry itself and I shall probably be sent abroad to a different destination. I'm adding all of this because it says here that I worked at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I still work at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not sure that this is recorded correctly. Your position in Berlin, you were deputy ambassador there; right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, deputy ambassador. Bosnia-Herzegovina, since it is a specific state of three peoples, it always had three key diplomats. That is to say that one person would be an ambassador and the other two would be deputy ambassadors. They would have different ethnic backgrounds, and I as a Serb was deputy ambassador while my ambassador was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, Mr. Milinic, I'd like to advise you to put a pause between the question and answer and please speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I know, I work in the diplomatic service, I know what the problems of interpretation are. I shall do my best to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are eight associated exhibits, four of which are not on our Rule 65 ter list and we would ask that they be added as we hadn't incorporated an interview with Mr. Milinic until after the list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say eight items?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, seven items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any objections, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I draw your attention, Mr. Robinson, to the item that is referred to in para 26, that is 65 ter 22016. In the view the Chamber, the witness merely says he has been shown this document and -- without offering any substantive comment on this document. So as such, the Chamber is of the view that it does not form an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. Otherwise, the Chamber is satisfied with the requirements of the associated exhibits, so we'll admit the 92 ter statement as well as the other six associated exhibits. Shall we assign the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's 92 ter statement 1D9600 will be Exhibit D3682, and the six associated exhibits as listed in the 92 ter notifications will be Exhibits D3683 through to Exhibit D3688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Milinic's statement. [In English] Gordan Milinic is a lawyer who served as security advisor to the president of the Republika Srpska from February 1994 to December 1995. He later served as ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Russia and other diplomatic positions. While working as the president's security advisor during July 1995, Ambassador Milinic reviewed the reports of the security services of the Ministry of Interior as well as of the reports of the security organs of the Main Staff of VRS on a daily basis. None of those -- these reports made any reference to the killings of prisoners from Srebrenica. Ambassador Milinic was aware -- unaware of the killing of prisoners from Srebrenica in July 1995. He believes that President Karadzic was also unaware of such killings. Ambassador Milinic worked closely with President Karadzic and observed his relations with his subordinates. President Karadzic displayed trust in his subordinates. When presented with a document for his signature, President Karadzic received an oral explanation about what the document was about and rarely read documents presented for his signature, such as directive 7. Ambassador Milinic began working for the Presidency around the time of the first Markale shelling in February 1994, and was also working for the Presidency when the second Markale shelling took place in August 1995. The information reported to the Presidency on both occasions was that the Bosnian Serbs had not fired the shells which exploded at the market. Ambassador Milinic was aware of the relations between President Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb Army. He believes that President Karadzic had a difficult time asserting his authority over the army and notes that he tried to dismiss General Mladic on more than one occasion without success. Ambassador Milinic knows Radovan Karadzic's attitude towards the war and the plight of civilians. President Karadzic never favoured the forced expulsion of civilians and used his influence whenever possible to see that civilians were treated humanely and in compliance with the Geneva Conventions. [Interpretation] Now I would kindly ask for this document to be called up, I have a question for Ambassador Milinic in relation to this document that was not admitted as an associated exhibit, 65 ter 22016.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you remember this? Do you remember this letter that you sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. This letter speaks of disobedience of the military organs vis-a-vis the president of the republic, that is to say, soldiers had looted a gasoline station. Also, there was a blockade of traffic in Brcko. This was done via the soldiers of the VRS, the civilian police is not in charge. They could not intervene. But the military security organs did not take any measures whatsoever. We urgently sent a letter here to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and yet again we did not receive any information as to the taking of any kind of measures vis-a-vis the perpetrators of such crimes. For me this was total disobedience and I informed the president of the republic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what document is linked to this letter of yours. Do you remember what this is? It's not very legible in Serbian, but perhaps we can also use the English.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. Oh, I see. English. Yes, let's try. Let's try to read this. I cannot. I really cannot find my way here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Second paragraph, seizing alcohol, shops and unprofessional contact by soldiers and military conscripts had also been documented and so on.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. Alcohol. I see that. Indeed. There were so many problems in the relations between the Main Staff and President Karadzic. This was one of the problems. I don't remember exactly now. I don't remember this particular case. Well, this is a case of lack of military discipline. You always reacted when there was such lack of discipline, and you asked for that to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you tell us whether each and every incident reached me or whether you made a selection in terms of what you would communicate to me and according to which criteria if there was a selection carried out?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I made an effort, because you were so very busy and you had such a lot of work as president of the republic, and as for all smaller things, I tried to have that resolved without you. And, yes, I did make some kind of a selection. However, we did not have any authority vis-a-vis the Main Staff. We could only use you. We the civilian authorities could only use you so that you could send an order to the Main Staff so that they react to such things. And all my experience, and indeed I have such a lot of experience, is that you're a man who did not [Realtime transcript read in error "did for the"] command the Army of Republika Srpska. The Main Staff did not respect you at all. They were a clique of generals who worked on their own and they used you only as a cover. You were a cover, a screen for them, and they just asked you to provide them with money, fuel, and everything else you needed. That is my impression. I am a man who knows all the secrets in Republika Srpska at that time. It's been 20 years now. I remember quite a few things. It is sad that that is what the truth was but that is what the truth was. You tried to put an end to that. You tried to dismiss the military leadership, but you could not do that. I always remember the session of the National Assembly when Pantelija Milovanovic, a member of parliament, spoke and said: The Supreme Commander should be the Supreme Commander. Let us take some measures so that the Supreme Commander really commands this army. This army is not being commanded by Radovan Karadzic. Ah, all right. Another member of parliament, I'd just like to say what he said. Gentlemen, I would like to inform you that General Bozo Novak, before a line of soldiers openly says, Radovan Karadzic is not our commander and the Main Staff does not recognise Radovan Karadzic as its commander. So this is what members of parliament said in the National Assembly. I was present there, and you have all the records and you can find these details as well. Everybody saw that something was wrong, that something wasn't going right, but the president was powerless. Had Radovan Karadzic been asked, not a single person would have lost his life in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not a single person would have been killed. Radovan Karadzic was a person of peace. He went to peace conferences. He sought peaceful solutions. He always said, We, Serbs, fight with the left hand, like boxers do, who just defend themselves, and we are waiting for peace and we're asking for peace. That is the main thing that our president focused on all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, we see two letters here in this document. Do you know how they are related to each other? First one is dated 1st of September or -- 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th of September, yes. This is my letter dated the 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And second one is 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I really cannot read this second letter. It may be an answer to my request. This is about an incident in Brcko, the blockade of traffic and the robbery of the gas station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the second page. Any objection, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. On page 66, line 22, you're recorded as having said: [In English] "You are a man who did for the command." Who did not command. [Interpretation] What exactly did you say? I believe that you heard the interpretation but you speak English.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 22, of course you cannot scroll up, it says that: "You are a man who did for the command," and I remember you saying "did not for the command."

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: You mean about you. I said that you did not command the VRS and I'm convinced that it's the case. I was with you every day. I was involved in all matters on a daily basis. I'm a man who received all strictly confidential information. I am a man who knew everything. It is a pity that the truth was such and that I now must bring everything to light what happened to -- in the leadership. But there were cases when the fighters in the trenches got flyers against the civilian leadership of the VRS. I took part in international seminars and I know what civilian control of the armed forces is. In the Republika Srpska that did not exist. The civilian authorities did not control the military structures, nor was it able to. This man here tried to replace the commander three times. He wanted to change the composition of the Main Staff three times, and each time the Main Staff was too powerful, and it had weapons so that the president of the republic could not replace the people from the Main Staff. At any rate, they gathered and organised a protest against the president and said that they do not recognise, they do not acknowledge the document replacing the commander. And they continued to command as a -- as an independent body. They just needed the civilian authorities as a pretext, and then they would return to the auspices of the National Assembly and say, yes, we work for the people. We work for the National Assembly. Whereas, in fact, these generals who had been raised from all over the place were members of various parties. The Serbian Democratic Party did not act during the war. It was -- their members worked illicitly. There were people who were members of the Yugoslav left. That was the party of Milosevic's wife and other parties. They had their own programmes and they didn't care about the wishes, the orders and the suggestions of the civilian authorities of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. There will be more -- you will get an opportunity to say more. I have no further questions at this moment. [In English] There will be more opportunity -- okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been in its most part admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to return to your statement, paragraph 10, which you describe your role as a security advisor. Your job was to communicate information to the president so that he was kept informed on the events on the ground throughout the RS. That was the core of your work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The core of my work isn't really stated in any of these documents but I was in military intelligence, which means that before the war I worked for the Military Intelligence Service together with Major Fikret Muslimovic. Before the war, when the multi-party system came into being in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Fikret Muslimovic called me a Chetnik because I was a Serb and I called him an Ustasha as he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause a minute, please. I'm just going to ask you to direct your attention to my questions because we don't have that much time. So I want to ask you about the period not before the war but during the war and we're talking about the period in which you served as security advisor to the then president of the RS. That's the period we're concerned about. Now paragraph 10 you describe that job, and you say that the means by which you got information for the president was through the DB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: What I've just said, that I was in military intelligence, I should have told you more about that job. You know what intelligence services are. You know what the CIA is, and that every army has its own intelligence service as does every state. The RS had the state security sector. That was the civilian intelligence service which had its regional offices throughout the RS. All the territory was covered with agencies. Intelligence work comprises thousands of agents in -- everywhere. So had the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, we -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: -- military intelligence service --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, we know what intelligence agencies are. So let's just get back to the question. Your job was to communicate information you received from the DB; is that correct? That is what you say at paragraph 10 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: That is correct. My job was to be in the position of information from all security services in the RS, from state security and from military security, and to make them -- make this information available to President Karadzic, Deputy President Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic. I worked for the entire Presidency, and before each important meeting, President Koljevic would come to me for information, to get the latest information. The military intelligence was information from our spies about the movements of the enemy, where the enemy units are, what was going on. That was mostly what they were into.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause -- pause please.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you're saying now you received information both from the DB and also from the VRS Main Staff intelligence and security sector. Is that what you're saying? Those are the sources of your information which you then communicated to the president; right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Correct. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, as one of his advisors you were a close and trusted member of the president's -- then president's inner circle during the war. In 1995, let's say.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for the entire Presidency of the RS. I was the hub to which all intelligence came.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I had to be a highly informed man.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You remained in his service, the accused's service even after he left office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: No. I went to foreign affairs, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the RS. I was assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, in 1997, you and other employees of his office, of the president's office, you were assigned to the newly formed department for special purposes, weren't you? And that was located where the president's -- the former president's office had been in the Famos factory in Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: None of that is correct. Here is how it went: After President Karadzic left, I became assistant minister of foreign affairs of the RS, and after that, Dayton united us into a joint Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Hang on a minute. You were appointed assistant minister in October 1997; is that correct? When you were appointed, October 1997?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period prior to that. Let's move on. Let's move on. I'm now asking you to look at a document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 25233, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were aware of a RS police investigation into the disappearance of the RS presidential archives, the investigation that took place in 2004, were you? You don't need to look at the screen. You can just answer my question, please. Yes?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I got a letter while I was ambassador to Moscow. The Ministry of the Interior asked me whether I knew the whereabouts of those archives. I replied that I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you about this investigation. So you knew about the investigation, and you can see here that this is a preliminary report related to that investigation. And you were aware of that, were you?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got an official letter in Moscow. I was officially informed, and I officially replied that I knew nothing of those archives because I had gone to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. My official transfer was signed by Biljana Plavsic and the date was the 10th of January, 1997. That's when she officially --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause a moment. You were officially --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: -- transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- appointed as the assistant minister in October 1997. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to repeat your question, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were appointed as the assistant of the minister in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in October 1997. That's right, isn't it? Just to get the dates right. Yes?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, but an official who was relieved from his post is entitled to leave and pay even after the cessation of service. I was receiving pay from the Presidency until the whole business was over. That is the absence -- during the absence of an official after the expiry of his term in office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just wanted to quickly refer you to a section of this document. It's page 2 in fact of the English which isn't shown on the screen. It goes over on to page 2. Just page 1 here of the B/C/S that you see on the screen, and you see here that -- that this report identifies three persons as the persons in charge of the archive, the presidential archive for -- which disappeared in 1998. And you're one of those three persons, aren't you, at point -- at paragraph 3, you're identified there. You'd agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm mentioned there, but at the time I already worked for foreign affairs in Sarajevo even. It was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since 1998 or as of 1998, I was with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I travelled all over the world. Actually, I worked in Vienna, not in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I was -- I worked at an out-of-country voting centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6397, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to ask you to look at another document, please. This is 65 ter 25234. Now we're still on the presidential archives and the investigation into their disappearance. You know, don't you, that the content of those archives, the content of those archives -- you don't need to look at the screen yet. You can listen to the question. They included army --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They included army and state security documents, didn't they? Military and also DB documents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: All documents I worked with, the top secret ones, couldn't stay in offices long. Immediately after processing those documents were returned to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: The confidential archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And these are the documents that were in the archives, the state security documents, the military documents, to which you've been referring; right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These documents had to be archived in a top secret archive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we're also talking about the VRS security organs, those documents too are archived in the presidential archive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each highly confidential document sent to the president of the republic had it be returned to the archives of strictly confidential documents and couldn't be kept in offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you're aware, perhaps you're not, that in this case the Court has heard evidence that when ICTY investigators were in Pale in 1998 for purposes of searching the presidential archives, this is prior to their disappearance, a number of documents were hidden. They'd been removed. Are you aware of that evidence that's been heard before this Court?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I am only familiar with 1995 and 1996. There were investigators of the Tribunal coming and the entire archives were placed at their disposal. They worked for days copying whatever they were interested in and they were allowed to view everything. I kept running into them into the hallways. Everything was allowed to them. It was at the time when I was working for the service of the president. I kept meeting them. They worked there, photocopied there, everything was allowed. I don't know about 1998, though, because by that time I no longer worked for the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not going to call it up, Mr. President, but I'm referring to exhibit -- prior Exhibit number P03 -- sorry, 03932, paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now let us look, please, at this document that's on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like if we could move, please, on the English to page 6; in the B/C/S page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is the report of the investigation conducted by the RS MUP on the disappearance of the archives in 1998 and I'm just going to refer you, please, to one paragraph here at this page. And in the English you can see that paragraph starts: "Working in the [indiscernible] service," describing the people who in 1997 were working for the newly formed office for special purposes, and you can see there that your name is included within that list of persons. In the B/C/S you can also see, as you read down the page, the penultimate paragraph of the page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I see it. This man could have encountered me when I visited occasionally. I told you, at the time, on the 10th of January, I was already relieved of my duties in the service of the president. That was 1997. By that time I had already started working for the foreign office and I was still on the payroll of the Presidency as an official no longer within his term of mandate. I was engaged actually in the foreign office of Republika Srpska and I was preparing a seminar for diplomats in Bijeljina in the summer of 1997 as new diplomats of the RS were being trained to assume their positions in the joint foreign office of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: That was my job, and perhaps now and then I dropped by to see the guys.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to move please to the conclusions of this report which appear at page -- substantively at page 14 of the English, 14 and 15, as we start at 14. And in the B/C/S, please, at page 10. And you can see there -- you can see there at page 10 that the report is concluding -- making conclusions about these missing archives. And it says at -- at paragraph 5, a part of the documentation reached the territory of the Republic of Serbia and is being used by the committee for the defence of Radovan Karadzic for writing their books and documents. That's paragraph 5, and that's on page 14 of the English. And if we could move in the English to page 15, staying -- and the B/C/S, please, at page 11. You can see here two areas identified. In English it's the second area. But the two areas which need to be identified as a focus of investigation, the first being to further investigate Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, and secondly, a second hypothesis, which is that people close to Radovan Karadzic or his security moved the documentation from the official premises of the Presidency to a certain passive location and that they gave a part of the documentation, and so it goes on, to the committee for the defence of Radovan Karadzic headed by Kosta Cavoski and so on. So these are the various hypotheses of RS MUP as to where the presidential archives went. You were aware of these findings, were you, at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know at all where it is. I know that Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, indeed dropped by because he was the chief of police of the RS. I met him at Pale because at the time I worked for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs we knew each other. I know he came to the premises but I really don't know whether he took anything with him. I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please. The whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document nor does it contradict his testimony. In addition, this is a document which I believe should have been disclosed to us a very long time ago in connection with testimony of a Prosecution witness, and we will have -- be looking into the issue of A disclosure violation but we can put that aside for the moment, but what this witness has said about this document doesn't justify its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, the document does contradict the witness's testimony to the extent that he -- it is talking about an office for special purposes which is set up in 1997 or thereabouts following the accused's departure from office and it is an office of which this witness is said in the document to be part. I'm afraid I'm unable to deal with the allegation of disclosure violation in that is perhaps something that will be addressed in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Where it says -- where it says the special office for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first I hear of that office for special purposes. It sounds a bit funny.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In English it's at page 6 and it's the third from bottom paragraph, the bottom sentence, and in the B/C/S, similarly you can see it -- it's at page 5 of the B/C/S in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It says service for special -- service [Interpretation] As part of the state security. It's not in office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6398, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would only admit those two paragraphs. To admit this document for that limited purpose is really unfair. This is a document with a lot of allegations and information and this would really be unfair to admit all of this for this one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those pages shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the only thing that should be admitted is this page or if you want to admit the cover sheet. The other page that was shown to the witness, he didn't have any -- don't contradict him and he didn't have any substantive comment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to respond. There were -- there were the conclusions that I also read, so it was the -- it was the paragraphs relating to the office and then the conclusions later which were put to the witness and he, in fact, did respond to the content, not all of it, didn't agree with all of it, didn't disagree with all of it, but certainly there is a basis for admission of the conclusions also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can clarify? This is the first time I heard of this service for special purposes. What is it? I didn't work there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if you're going to rule against us, would you please look at lines 14 through 18 to see what the witness said about the conclusions before you do. Page 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the fact that these conclusions are basically hypotheses, would this have any bearing on -- on the question of admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think that definitely diminishes the weight if you find it admissible but the question that's before you, I think, is: What did this witness say about that portion of the document and whether that is sufficient comment on the document or contradiction of -- or the document contradicts his testimony to be admissible in the first place. And I don't think they've met that standard. If they didn't meet that standard, then the question of the hypothesis becomes the issue of the weight of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, because this involves a -- I apologise for that, but this is a matter that's come up time and time again and I just want to point out one aspect of what I consider to be Mr. Robinson's argument and that is when he acknowledges, and sometimes he hasn't, the fact that part of admissibility can depend upon contradiction that he sometimes tries to limit it to the contradiction of what the witness has said at that -- in that particular narrow portion. But of course, it's contradiction of the witness's overall testimony including aspects of his statement and those portions of the Defence position to which the witness has given support, and that's quite a different matter. Narrowly defining it, as Mr. Robinson often tries to do, is not fair, not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's nothing not statement about the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber by majority will not accept this, with me dissenting. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It remains the case, though, that the two pages are admitted is -- is that right, Mr. President? But just not the whole of the document? Sorry, the one page. [Microphone not activated] That was page [overlapping speakers] -- in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The majority is fine with accepting one page. We gave a ruling, Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to respond to something else which I consider to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document was disclosed more than two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The information that Mr. Reid had sent me when I inquired was it was disclosed as part of the Rule 66(B) material for this witness which came just a few months ago, but perhaps it had also been disclosed earlier so I'll look into that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6398, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you -- you said this afternoon you were the man who knew everything, and you were close to the accused and communicated with him even after his departure from office about his archives, about documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat yet again. I was security advisor to the Presidency of Republika Srpska. The Presidency entails the president of the RS, Dr. Radovan Karadzic; Deputy President Professor Nikola Koljevic; and Deputy President Biljana Plavsic. You can see that I was employed by Biljana Plavsic until the 10th of January, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That is not the question I asked you and I'd be grateful if you would focus on my questions and -- and try to answer my questions so that we can proceed in an effective --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Please repeat, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. So the question was whether or not you communicated with the accused after his departure from office, from the office of president, about his archives, the presidential archives, and about documents. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the question is precise, and my answer will be as precise. No. On the topic of archives and documents, I did not communicate any further. First of all, you keep insisting on some kind of personal relationship of mine with President Karadzic, but then you need to insist on my relationship with both Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic because I worked for them as well. It was the Presidency of the RS. I also worked for Biljana Plavsic not only for Radovan Karadzic. I was Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause -- pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: -- advisor until the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're testifying in these proceedings against this accused so I'm asking you questions about this accused. Okay? So your evidence is that you never communicated with the accused about documents, about the archives. Did he communicate to you about documents, about his archives after he had left office? It's a reasonably simple question.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. No. Yes. Radovan Karadzic withdrew from all positions in order not to damage the reputation of Republika Srpska. Holbrooke threatened with doing away with the RS and the SDS. And he withdrew and he stood by it. He didn't do anything after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, could you please concentrate on answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So your answer was: "Yes. No. Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what was your question. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you communicate with the accused about documents -- sorry. The question then was: Did the accused communicate with you about his archives, about documents, after he'd left office?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: On the topic of the archives and documents, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have up, please, 65 ter 21583. Now we've got this document both in B/C/S and in English, and it's just the first page of both English and B/C/S versions of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now I want to you look closely at the document on the screen. Look, please, at the header and you can see there to whom this document is addressed. Can you identify the names that appear there on the top?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Mira and Milijana were -- and Saska were the secretaries. This document never reached me. I've never seen it before. By that time I worked intensively for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and I was difficult to find. I was in Vienna in the out-of-country voting centre. This document has never reached me. I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Of course you don't deny that it's addressed to you. You're one of the addressees along with General Subotic and members of the -- former members of the office of the former president. It's dated 9th December 1997 --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: No, you're wrong. [In English] No, you are not right. You are not right. You are not right. [Interpretation] You're wrong because the document was addressed to Mira, Milijana and Saska, and then General Subotic and Mr. Gordan Milinic should be included if located. I wasn't located because I was in Vienna or wherever. So it was addressed to the secretaries, Mira, Miljana, and Saska. And it says "include" [In English] to involve if you can Mr. -- General Subotic and Mr. Milinic. [Interpretation] I was not found and I was not involved. I was deeply involved by that time with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I was a controller in the out-of-country voting centre in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Milinic, could you read out the first three lines in B/C/S. Read slow. Za Milosa -- could you read it. Read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slowly. So that we can hear. Could you read? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Milos, Mira, Milijana, Saska and include also General Subotic and Mr. Gordan Milinic. That's it. Include if they could locate us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You didn't read out the whole of the first part of the -- the document, did you? You stopped. Now I want you to, please, perhaps do that exercise again, if you don't mind, Mr. President. Can you read out, please, the whole of that first section in B/C/S so we can just be sure that we've got it right. All of it.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is added is the other implementers need not be included but issued tasks instead, that is to say, if they needed someone else's assistance in their work. That's what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this document gives various different tasks to different people, and some of those people aren't identified as -- as people to whom the letter is addressed at the top there. They're just identified in the body of the letter, but let's put that to one side. Can we go down, please, to one, two, three, four -- fourth paragraph, fourth paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask what this document is? Is there some kind of sign, signature, anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So we're looking, please, at the paragraph that I -- I referred you to. "It is very important when it comes to Srebrenica that I see the document first by which I appoint Mr. Deronjic civilian commissioner, and I think that was after our army's entry into the town. It is important to see with what tasks he was appointed and the original should be in our archive. However, the original of his agreement with the Muslim civilian together with the testimony of the UNPROFOR officer must be with him, so he should be asked to bring it, and he does not have to meet with them." Just pausing there, he's talking about meeting with investigators there from the ICTY, isn't he? Deronjic meeting with investigators from the ICTY in December 1997. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. No idea about this letter, about these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's just go to the bit that concerns you at the end of this paragraph, please. "When it comes to Deronjic and Bratunac, Bratunac, G. Milinic can arrange it that someone from the DB go and return with the original in three hours. Although Deronjic should not be afraid to come. He does not even have to meet with him, and if he does, that cannot be bad for him," and so it goes on. So these were instructions to you to arrange to get someone from the DB to go and get an original document from Bratunac from Deronjic. Is that something you remember being instructed to do?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I did not receive any such instructions. No one found me with regard to this document. I don't know who wrote this. I don't know what this is. I don't know what this is all about. I don't find this clear at all. I did not have any contact with this, who this is who is mentioning my name, who is writing this. I do not find that clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: But this --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This document is from the accused, isn't it? It's from the accused. Just read it and you can see that it's from the accused. It's talking about his defence and addressed to his close associates, talking about Ljiljana getting -- going through the folders at home. He's talking -- it's from the accused, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: Give me the rest of the text. Give me the rest of the text. Is there a signature of his there? Give me the text further on. This is just one page. I don't find that clear that this comes from the accused. Let me see the rest of the text. Let me see if there's a signature or anything there. Maybe this is a forgery. How should I know who wrote this? This is the first time I see this. I don't know what this is all about. No one ever contact me -- contacted me in relation to this. No one. Ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Who appointed Deronjic civilian commissioner? It says: I appointed -- I appoint Deronjic civilian commissioner. He's talking about that document. Who -- who made that appointment? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: [In English] It was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Who made the appointment?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was appointed either by the government or the president of the republic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It was the accused --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: -- but that was -- that was -- that was 1995, sometime in August, September. Somebody appointed him civilian commissioner. I believe it was the president who appointed him, but this was a legal act by the legal government for establishing civilian authority. I remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking for details --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: -- that in 1995 Deronjic worked on establishing the civilian authorities in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're an intelligent man. You're looking at a letter that's addressed to you that you apparently didn't receive in Vienna and it's talking about the appointment of Deronjic by the writer of this letter as civilian commissioner, and I'm asking you whether or not this letter is from the accused.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC
utterances.text: I cannot establish on the basis of anything that this comes from the accused. I have already told you that this is the first time I see this letter, and I have no idea what this is all about. Now that I read it I see that it has to do with Deronjic. I know that sometime from August, September 1995, Deronjic was commissioner for organising civilian life in Srebrenica. That I know. That I remember. But this letter, I have no idea. You know what that means? I have no idea. I've never seen it. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President. And if I may just deal with the genesis of the document, I can deal with that briefly. I have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a question for Mr. Robinson. I note Mr. Karadzic's intervention, I quote: "May I ask what that document is? Is there some kind of sign, signature, anything?" Lines 10 and 11 on page 86. Is the -- is the Defence case, is it the Defence case that Mr. Karadzic had nothing to do with this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we haven't -- we've just seen this letter and we haven't discussed that, but I don't think that's the Defence case. The Defence case is -- we're going to state our position as respect to this admissibility of this letter, and if we have any evidence to lead about the letter, we'll do so in due course, but we're not either affirming or denying who the author was and we're not required to at this point.
